opus-5.5.text:
It's a really important part of our story, and honestly, it's something I think about a lot. Before Cohere for AI existed in its current form, there was For AI, which was this very grassroots, decentralized community of researchers. It started from a pretty simple observation: there are a lot of talented people around the world who want to do machine learning research but don't have access to the traditional entry points. They're not sitting inside a big industry lab, they're not necessarily at a top-tier university, and so the question was, how do you create a space where they can still collaborate, get mentorship, and publish meaningful work?

So when Cohere for AI launched, I really saw it as a continuation of that spirit rather than a replacement. We kept that open, community-driven DNA at the heart of what we do. A big part of our structure is still this open science community, where people from dozens of countries join, propose projects, find collaborators, and work together across time zones and institutions. That's very much inherited from For AI.

What changed is that we now have more resources behind it. We can offer compute, we can support a dedicated research team, and we can run programs like our scholars program that give people a structured on-ramp into research. So it's a hybrid model: a core research lab doing fundamental work, alongside a much broader open community that feeds ideas, talent, and perspectives into everything we do.

And for me, that combination matters a lot, because I think some of the most interesting questions in machine learning right now, things like multilingual models, efficiency, and who gets to participate in building these systems, really benefit from having a wider set of people at the table. The decentralized roots of For AI are a big reason why we approach research the way we do today.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to describe it is that For AI was really the seed of what Cohere for AI became. For AI started as this independent, decentralized research collective — it was something Aidan, Nick, and Ivan were involved in, along with a group of us who felt that a lot of important research wasn't happening in traditional institutions, and that there was a huge pool of talent that didn't have access to a well-resourced lab. The idea was very simple: you don't need to be at a big industrial lab or a top university to do meaningful work, and if we could lower the barrier to entry, a lot of good things would follow.

When we launched Cohere for AI, we really carried that DNA forward, but with a few important differences. One is that we now have a core team of full-time researchers, which lets us go deep on long-horizon problems — things like our work on multilingual models, or on understanding the dynamics of how models learn and fail. That's hard to sustain in a purely volunteer setting. The second is that we've been able to invest much more seriously in the open science community side. We have a Scholars Program, we run these community research groups, we hold open reading groups — and that's where the decentralized spirit really lives on. It's thousands of people across many countries collaborating on research, often meeting each other for the first time in a Discord channel.

So I'd say the relationship is one of continuity rather than a break. The values are the same: open, collaborative, and focused on broadening who gets to participate in fundamental research. What's changed is that we now have the resources and stability to do that at scale, and to pair the community with a dedicated research lab that's working on some of the hardest problems in the field. I actually think that pairing is one of the most interesting things about it — the full-time team and the broader community end up feeding into each other in ways that neither could do alone.

There are talented people everywhere, but access to research opportunities is much more uneven.

Cohere for AI carries that motivation forward: how do we create a community where people with different backgrounds can work together on meaningful research? Having an institutional home gives us a way to support that work, while preserving the openness and sense of belonging that made the decentralized community valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a continuation of the same idea. For AI started as a decentralized research community, bringing together people who were excited about machine learning but didn’t necessarily have a conventional route into research. And that experience really shaped what we wanted to build with Cohere for AI.

Research talent is distributed much more broadly than access to research opportunities. So the question was, how do we create a community where people can contribute, learn from one another, and do meaningful research, wherever they are? Cohere for AI gives us a way to support that vision with more resources and infrastructure, while preserving that open, community-driven spirit.
